'''''Lupinus albus''''', commonly known as the '''white lupin''', is a [[species]] of the [[genus]] ''[[Lupinus]]'' in the family [[Fabaceae]] native to the northeastern [[Mediterranean region]]. It is also a traditional [[Pulse (legume)|pulse]] cultivated across the Mediterranean region and elsewhere.

== Description ==
The white lupin is an annual, more or less [[Pubescent (botany)|pubescent]] plant that typically reaches 30 to 120 cm in height. It grows naturally throughout the [[Balkans]], the island of [[Sicily]], and [[Turkey]],<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=Plants of the World Online | website=Plants of the World Online | date=1968-12-18 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:504069-1 | access-date=2025-01-24}}</ref> and is also widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] across the Mediterranean region including North Africa, in Europe north to Great Britain, Germany, the Baltic States and western Russia, and also in the Indian subcontinent.<ref name="POWO"/> Naturalised populations are also known in Australia and Chile.<ref name="POWO"/> It is found in meadows, pastures, and grassy slopes on both sandy and acidic soil. The white lupin is cultivated throughout the Mediterranean region and in Egypt, Sudan, Ethiopia, Syria, Europe, South America, and tropical and southern Africa. The ancient cultivation of white lupin under the local name ''hanchcoly'' was practiced until recently in western [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]].{{citation needed|date=May 2024}} It is also sometimes known in cultivation as "field lupin",<ref>{{cite web | title=Field lupin | website=Biota of NZ | date=2001-08-17 | url=https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/vernacular-names/b1d683ff-e3fd-4886-9e73-cf5ba71cef43 | access-date=2025-01-24}}</ref> though this name is imprecise, having been applied to [[field lupin|several species]] in the genus.

White lupin is distinct within the large and polymorphous genus ''Lupinus'' for a small variation of morphological characteristics.{{which|date=May 2024}} However, the species has wide, intraspecific variability in physiological plant properties; the duration of vernalisation time and growth rate, photoperiodic sensitivity, shape tolerance, drought resistance, and cold- and winter-hardiness. There are winter and spring forms of white lupin. The duration of the growing period under spring sowing varies from 106 to 180 days, seed mass per plant varies from 2.2 g to 40 g, green mass yield per from 9 g to 250 g, protein content in the seed from 35.0% to 53.7%, and oil content from 6.2% to 12.0%.{{citation needed|date=May 2024}}

== History and modern uses ==
[[File:Lupinus albus.JPG|left|222 px|thumb|''Lupinus albus'' beans, cooked and preserved in brine.]]

The beginning of lupin cultivation in the Old World is sometimes associated with [[Ancient Egypt]].<ref name="zhukov">{{cite journal |last1=Zhukovsky |first1=P. M. |title=A contribution to the knowledge of genus Lupinus Tourn |journal=Bull. Appl. Bot. Genet. Plant Breed |date=1929 |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=16–294}}</ref> It is more likely, however, that white lupin was originally introduced into cultivation in ancient Greece, where its greatest biodiversity was concentrated and where wild-growing forms have been preserved until today (ssp. ''graecus'').<ref name="kurlovich">{{cite book |last1=Kurlovich |first1=B. S. |title=Lupins: geography, classification, genetic resources, and breeding |date=2002 |publisher=Pub. House "Intan" |location=St. Petersburg |isbn=5-86741-034-X |url=https://lupins-bk.blogspot.com/2006/07/eco-geographic-classification-of_17.html |access-date=11 May 2024}}</ref> On the Balkan Peninsula, representatives of another subspecies of white lupin (ssp. ''termis'' and ssp. ''albus'') turned wild and now grow in natural environments. Also, the Grecian genesis of cultivated lupin may be testified by lupin's Greek name ''thermos'', which translates roughly to "hot".<ref name="kurlovich" /> White lupin dispersed from Greece to adjacent regions and states over time, particularly Egypt and Ancient Rome. The forms of lupin with white seeds and pink-and-blue or light-pink flowers (''L. termis'') spread mainly towards the south (Egypt, Libya, and Palestine), while the forms with white seeds and grayish-blue or white flowers (''L. albus'') moved to the west ([[Apennine Peninsula]] and beyond).<ref>{{cite web|author=BK |url=https://lupins-bk.blogspot.com/2006/07/history-of-lupin-domestication.html |title=lupins-bk.blogspot.com/2006/07/history-of-lupin-domestication.html |publisher=Lupins-bk.blogspot.com |date=2006-07-17 |access-date=2012-08-04}}</ref>

According to Zohary and Hopf, "even today the white lupin is an appreciated food crop and it is still cultivated in some Mediterranean countries—particularly Egypt."<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Zohary |first1=Daniel |title=Domestication of plants in the old world: the origin and spread of cultivated plants in West Asia, Europe, and the Nile Valley |last2=Hopf |first2=Maria |date=2000 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-850357-6 |edition=3rd |location=Oxford New York |page=123}}</ref> In [[Greece]], especially on the island of [[Crete]] and in the [[Peloponnese]] area, lupin seeds are a very common snack during [[Lent]]. They are normally soaked in seawater for 2–3 hours to mellow the flavour and are then consumed raw. In [[France]], [[Spain]], [[Portugal]], [[central Italy|central]] and [[southern Italy]], and parts of [[Brazil]], lupin is a very popular snack (''tramousse'' or ''lupin'' in French, ''lupini'' in Italian, ''tremoços'' in Portuguese, ''altramuces'' or ''chochos'' in Spanish, ''tramussos'' in Catalan). Lupin is known in Arabic as ''ترمس'' ''termes'', and the seeds are sold as a popular street snack in [[Egypt]] after being soaked and brined.

== Cultivation ==
Since ancient times, white lupin has been widespread in the Mediterranean region and in the Middle East due to its high tolerance for acidic soils and its soil-restoration abilities.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.agraria.org/coltivazionierbacee/lupino.htm|title=Lupino - Lupinus spp.|website=Istruzione agraria online}}</ref> It tolerates a soil acidity up to pH = 6.5, while [[alkaline]] or organic soils are not suitable for growth.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://shop.fibl.org/chen/mwdownloads/download/link/id/104/|title=Merkblatt Biolupinen|website=Forschungsinstitut für biologischen Landbau (FiBL)}}</ref> The soil must be well drained and loose because lupin is subject to root asphyxia.<ref name=":2" /> White lupin flourishes in the same climate zones as maize, although lupin, except at the beginning of the growing season, requires little water thanks to its long tap root.<ref name=":3" />

=== Sowing ===
In hotter climate zones, such as in Italy, sowing occurs following plowing in October–November in order to bury the stubble of the previous crop (often a cereal.) Due to its branched structure, lupin can adapt to different sowing densities, compensating for a lower density with a higher branch growth.<ref name=":2" /> In colder zones where lupin cannot survive the winter, white lupin is sowed in the spring, typically between March and April. The soil must be prepared as soon as possible after the last frost of the winter. The seedbed must be sufficiently fine, particularly in organic farming where mechanical weeding is done (so that harrowing the displacement of clods does not harm the plants). In regions where lupin is not indigenous, if it is cultivated for the first time in a soil or if the soil pH is higher than 6.5, lupin seeds must be inoculated with the nitrogen-fixing bacterium ''Rhizobium lupini''. Soil acidity is an important factor for nitrogen fixation.<ref name=":3" />

=== Fertilisation ===
Due to its symbiosis with nitrogen-fixing bacteria, white lupin does not need nitrogen fertilisation, though it requires about 40 kg/ha of P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> and 60 kg/ha of K<sub>2</sub>O. Due to its long tap root, white lupin can exploit phosphorus reserves in the soil. The crop rotation for white lupin ideally lasts at least four or five years, and lupin is often grown after a cereal crop. Lupin is a good preculture since it leaves about 50 kg/ha of nitrogen in the field.<ref name=":3" />

=== Weed control ===
Lupin does not compete well with weeds, particularly in the colder zones, because it only produces sufficient foliage to shade out weeds in late summer. Mechanical weeding is feasible, as is hoeing if the rows are wide enough.<ref name=":3" /> Chemical weeding is also used, by means of herbicides applied for other grain legumes.<ref name=":2" />

=== Yield ===
Depending on the climate zone of cultivation, pods ripen sometime between late June and late August. Seeds do not ripen all at once and are harvested when 90% of the pods are brown. To harvest with a combine harvester the ideal seed water content is 13-16%. Good yields are between 2 t/ha and 3.5 t/ha,<ref name=":3" /> although average yields are lower.<ref name=":2" />

== Diseases ==
As there are numerous diseases affecting ''Lupinus albus'', management is complex and important. Higher yields can be obtained by sowing early in the year, but this strategy can increase the impact of pests and diseases.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Joy|first=Robert|title=Plant Guide|journal=Usda NRCS|pages=5–8}}</ref>

Fungal diseases are often controlled with [[fungicide]]s.<ref name=":1" /> To control non-fungal diseases, the most effective practices are crop rotation and the use of disease-free seeds.<ref name=":1" />

===Fungi===
The following three fungi are lupin-specific and fully adapted to the presence of alkaloids:<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Huyghe|first=Christian|title=White Lupin (< I> Lupinus Albus L.)|journal=Field Crops Research|volume=53|issue=1–3|pages=147–160|doi=10.1016/S0378-4290(97)00028-2|year=1997|bibcode=1997FCrRe..53..147H }}</ref>

* ''Pleichaeta setosa'', which causes brown-leaf spot and can be combatted by selecting frost–tolerant plants
* ''Uromyces lupinicolus'', also known as rust, which causes defoliation and biomass reduction, and be treated with triazole fungicides
* ''[[Colletotrichum gloeosporioides]]'', a seed-borne disease<ref name=":0" /> which can kill lupin plants before they flower, resulting in a null yield,<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jansen|first=P. C. M.|title=Lupinus albus|journal=Protabase}}</ref> and which is mostly addressed via seed treatment<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Romer|first=P, K |display-authors=etal |title=Further trials to control Anthracnose (Colletotrichum sp.) in white lupins (Lupinus albus) with chemicals|journal=Proceeding 9th International Lupin Conference|pages=25–27}}</ref>

===Viruses===
Bean mosaic virus is transmitted by [[aphid]]s and infected seeds, and is the major viral disease for ''Lupinus albus''. A major disease for other [[Lupinus|lupins]] is [[cucumber mosaic virus]], but ''Lupinus albus'' is immune to it.<ref name=":1" />

===Pests===
''Phorbia platura'' is the only insect which has historically significantly impacted ''Lupinus albus.''<ref name=":0" /> Insect larvae may damage the roots and hypocotyls,<ref name=":0" /> and can be treated most effectively via soil insecticides or other seed treatments.<ref name=":0" />

''[[Aphid]]s'' are also a problem, particularly during the budding and early pod stages.<ref name=":1" /> They reduce crop yield, limit the number of flower blooms, and also {{Clarify span|lead to pod formation|date=March 2024}}.<ref name=":1" /> They can also transmit diseases.<ref name=":1" />

Other pests and detrimental organisms include:<ref name=":1" />
* bean seedling [[maggot]]s, which cause seedlings to wilt and die
* [[beetle]] and moth larvae, which kill seedlings
* [[slug]]s, which attack leaves
* [[thrips]], which attack flowers and leaves
* [[Mirid bugs|mired bugs]], which attack young seed pods
* budworms, which feed on pods and seeds

The chemical composition of lupin seeds depends on the cultivation region except for the protein content which is independent from environmental conditions. White lupin seeds contain a high amount of protein. The [[net protein utilisation]] is slightly lower than that of animal protein. The fats have a 2:1 ratio of [[Omega-6 fatty acid|omega-6]] (w-6) to [[Omega-3 fatty acid|omega-3]] (w-3), whereby [[oleic acid]] (w-9) accounts for about 50% of the fat. The carbohydrates found in the seeds are mainly [[Dietary fiber|soluble and insoluble fibre]] and the starch content is very low. Therefore, lupin seeds have a low [[Glycemic index|glycaemic index]]. The main macroelements found in white lupin seeds are [[Potassium|K]], [[Manganese|Mn]], and [[Magnesium|Mg]], and the prevailing microelements are [[Calcium|Ca]], [[Iron|Fe]], and [[Sodium|Na]].

The white lupin seeds have a low or very low content of [[antinutrient]]s. Their removal is possible through food processing treatments (e.g., dehulling, germinating, cooking, soaking, fermentation, and extraction). Total [[alkaloid]] content in sweet white lupin cultivars does not currently exceed 0.02%. Some of the sulphur-containing amino acids (about 4% of the proteins) may have an allergenic effect. The main [[allergen]]s are Lup-1 (a conglutin b, vicilin-like protein), and Lup-2 (conglutin a, legumin-like protein).

== Animal nutrition ==
{{Overly detailed|section|date=May 2024}}

=== Ruminants ===
Although an excessive use of ''L. albus'' or other [[Lupinus#Agriculture|lupin species]] can cause unwanted side-effects, this species may prove useful as a feeding supplement for livestock.<ref name=":0" /> While ''L. albus'' is used in Australia to provide sheep with protein in the form of a whole-grain feed supplement, there are concerns regarding product quality and safety. This is due to the susceptibility of some lupin cultivars towards ''[[Diaporthe toxica]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=LUAL22|title=Plants Profile for Lupinus albus (white lupine)|website=plants.usda.gov|access-date=2017-11-18}}</ref> This fungus can cause a fatal intoxication with lupin seed called [[lupinosis]], which appears to mainly affect sheep.<ref name=Williamson-eal-1994>{{cite journal |last1=Williamson |first1=P. M. |last2=Highet |first2=A. S. |last3=Gams |first3=W. |last4=Sivasithamparam |first4=K. |last5=Cowling |first5=W. A. |date=December 1994 |title=''Diaporthe toxica'' sp. nov., the cause of lupinosis in sheep |journal=Mycological Research |volume=98 |issue=12 |pages=1364–1368 |doi=10.1016/S0953-7562(09)81064-2 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0953756209810642/pdf |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

While there no major negative health effects have been found in cattle, it has been found that supplementation with ''L. albus'' can cause a decrease in milk protein concentration and milk protein yield in dairy cows.<ref name=":1" /> Nonetheless, roasted seeds of ''L. albus'' appear to be a good source of rumen protected fatty acids.<ref name=":1" />

=== Non-ruminants ===
Unlike its use with ruminants, ''L. albus'' should not be considered as an optimal feed for pigs. Research indicates that a diet based on white lupin results in poorer growth rates due to reduced feed intake when compared with other lupin species, such as ''[[Lupinus angustifolius|L. angustifolius]]''.<ref name=":0" /> Experiments have indicated that ingesting ''L. albus'' can affect digestibility and nutrient uptake in piglets negatively.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sujak|first1=Agnieszka|last2=Kotlarz|first2=Anna|last3=Strobel|first3=Wacław|title=Compositional and nutritional evaluation of several lupin seeds|journal=Food Chemistry|volume=98|issue=4|pages=711–719|doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2005.06.036|year=2006 |bibcode=2006FoodC..98..711S }}</ref>

Although [[broiler]]s can tolerate a high share of lupin seeds in their diet, excess use should be avoided, as it causes moist faeces that negatively affects hygiene and promotes health risks.<ref name=":0" /> It has been shown that ''L. albus'' has the potential to partly replace the use of [[soybean]] in poultry production.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Diaz|first1=Duarte|last2=Morlacchini|first2=Mauro|last3=Masoero|first3=Francesco|last4=Moschini|first4=Maurizio|last5=Fusconi|first5=Giorgio|last6=Piva|first6=Gianfranco|date=2006-01-01|title=Pea seeds (Pisum sativum), faba beans (Vicia faba var. minor) and lupin seeds (Lupinus albus var. multitalia) as protein sources in broiler diets: effect of extrusion on growth performance|journal=Italian Journal of Animal Science|volume=5|issue=1|pages=43–53|doi=10.4081/ijas.2006.43|doi-access=free}}</ref>

White lupin seeds have also been recommended as rabbit feed, and may prove useful as a partial replacement for fish meal or soybean meal in aquaculture.<ref>Heuzé V., Thiollet H., Tran G., Nozière P., Lessire M., Lebas F., 2018. White lupin (''Lupinus albus'') seeds. Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/279</ref>
